h1: Meaty and yeasty notes in beer: tasting yeast autolysis
title: Yeast Autolysis: Meaty and Yeasty Notes | Craft Beer School
desc: How to recognise yeast autolysis in beer: meaty, brothy, soy and rubbery notes, what causes them in the fermenter and how brewers prevent them.
teaser: A brothy, Marmite-like note in your lager is not a new hop. It is dead yeast talking.
standfirst: Yeast autolysis is the breakdown of yeast cells after they die. It leaves meaty, savoury and sometimes rubbery flavours in beer. It is easy to confuse with other yeast notes. In most styles it is a fault worth catching early.
sections:
The descriptors run from mild to severe. At low levels: bready, yeasty, slightly savoury. As it builds: meaty, brothy, beef stock, yeast extract spread, soy sauce. At its worst: rubbery, sulphury or a burnt-match note, sometimes with a soapy feel on the tongue.

Fresh yeast character is different. Young beer can smell of fresh bread dough or a bakery, which is not autolysis. Autolysis is the smell of yeast that has died and broken down, which is closer to a pot of stock than to a loaf.

Once fermentation ends, yeast settles to the bottom of the tank or the cone. The cells are starved and stressed. Over time some of them die. Their own enzymes then start to digest the cell from the inside. The cell walls break and release amino acids, nucleotides, fatty acids and other compounds into the beer.

Some of those compounds taste savoury in the same way a stock does. Fatty acids can bring soapy or goaty notes. Breakdown of sulphur compounds can give rubbery or meaty sulphur notes. Released fats also harm foam.

Autolysis speeds up with temperature, time and pressure. Yeast health matters too, which our guide to yeast viability and vitality covers.

• Leaving beer on a thick yeast cake for too long. Especially at fermentation temperature. A conical tank with a large compacted yeast bed is a classic risk.
  • Warm storage. A cone sitting at 20 °C or more after fermentation accelerates the process. In a hot brewery without good glycol control, this is common.
  • Tall tanks. Hydrostatic pressure in tall cylindroconical tanks stresses settled yeast. The yeast at the bottom of the cone also gets warmer than the rest of the tank, because it insulates itself.
  • Stressed or old yeast. Yeast that was unhealthy when pitched, or reused through many generations without care, dies faster.
  • Long bottle conditioning in heat. Bottle-conditioned beers stored warm for months can develop autolysis from the yeast in the bottle.
Preventing it on the brewery floor

The most direct control is removing yeast from the cone soon after fermentation. Many brewers dump or harvest yeast within a day or two after reaching final gravity and again after the diacetyl rest. If the cone has a cooling jacket, chilling it helps, since a warm yeast plug is where autolysis starts.

Crashing the beer cold after fermentation and the diacetyl rest slows yeast metabolism. Our guide to cold crashing explains the method and the timing. A crash to around 0 to 2 °C drops yeast out of suspension and lets you remove it from the cone.

Healthy pitching rates, good aeration of wort and controlled fermentation temperatures all produce stronger yeast, which lasts longer before dying.

Some styles carry a gentle yeasty character as part of their profile. Unfiltered German Kellerbier, some bottle-conditioned Belgian ales and certain hefeweizens can show a light bready, yeasty note. Aged champagne and some sparkling wines use controlled autolysis deliberately to build toasty, brioche-like flavours.

The line is crossed when the note becomes meaty, brothy, soy-like or rubbery. In a crisp lager or a hoppy IPA, any noticeable autolysis is a fault.

Do not confuse autolysis with sulphur from fermentation. Young lagers often carry a rotten egg or struck match note that fades with conditioning. Autolysis does not fade with time. It gets worse, because more yeast keeps breaking down.
Training the panel to recognise it

Autolysis is hard to describe until you have smelled it. A simple reference: dissolve a small amount of yeast extract spread in a neutral pale lager and taste it alongside the plain beer. Many commercial off-flavour kits also include autolysis or meaty references. Our guide to off flavour spiking kits covers the options.

Once your panel knows the note, add it to the release tasting sheet and taste every tank that has sat on yeast longer than planned. If the note appears, trace back: how long was the beer on the yeast, at what temperature and when was the cone last dumped? Linking a tasting note to a process step is the skill that makes a panel useful. It is also the part that needs practice with real samples, ideally with a group that can check each other's calls.
faqs: What is yeast autolysis in beer?
It is the breakdown of dead yeast cells, which releases compounds that give meaty, brothy, soy or rubbery flavours. It happens when beer sits too long on yeast, especially when warm.
Remove yeast from the cone promptly after fermentation, crash cool the beer and keep yeast healthy with good pitching and fermentation control.
Is yeasty flavour always a fault?
No. A light bready, yeasty note can suit some unfiltered or bottle-conditioned styles. Meaty, brothy or rubbery notes are a fault in almost any beer.
